slides: Let's continue with two more cases, and one more rule.

slides.say: A third case. Sometimes there are no letters at all, but an amount is unknown, and they ask for a ratio or a part. In a ratio, the actual numbers don't matter. One to two, two to four and ten to twenty are the same ratio.
at: One to two, two to four

slides.say: So I may choose the amount myself. For example, half of a number plus a third of the same number. What part of the number is it?
at: half of a number plus a third

slides.say: Which number? Six, because both two and three go into it. Half of six is three, and a third of six is two. Together five, out of six. So it's five sixths of the number, whatever the number is.
The fourth case. An equation, but with more letters than equations, and they ask for one value. For example, four x plus six y equals eighteen. What is six x plus nine y?

slides: One equation with two letters has many solutions. But they ask for one number, so it must come out the same for every solution. So I may take the easiest solution.

slides.say: I give one letter a value, and I solve the equation for the other. x equals zero, because zero kills a whole term. Then six y equals eighteen, so y is three.
at: I give one letter a value

slides.say: Now what they ask. Six times zero is zero, and nine times three is twenty-seven. So six x plus nine y is twenty-seven.

slides: Here zero is perfect, because the answer is a number, so there's nothing to tie. And I chose only x. If I chose both letters, the equation probably wouldn't hold.

slides.say: And it's really true. Six x plus nine y is one and a half times four x plus six y, because each part is one and a half times as big. And one and a half times eighteen is twenty-seven.
One more trick for choosing the number. In a story with letters, look for the value where nothing happens. Then you know the answer without any formula.
For example, n friends rent a boat for P shekels and share the cost. Then k more friends join, and they share it again. By how much less does each one pay?
Plug in k equals zero. Nobody joined, so nobody pays less, and the answer must be zero. So every choice that doesn't give zero when k is zero is out, with no calculation at all.
This value often leaves two choices. Then use a tie-breaker, an ordinary number like k equals one, and check only the two that are left.
Last, questions about what is always true, or not always true. To show that something is not always true, one example where it fails is enough.

For example, is a squared plus b squared always equal to the bracket a plus b, squared? Let a equal one and b equal two, two small, different numbers. One plus four is five, and three squared is nine. Five is not nine, so it's not always true. One counterexample, and we're done.

But always is different. A few examples that work don't prove always, because the next number might fail. In a question with choices, we don't prove it. We rule out the other three choices, and the one that's left is the answer.

So, when do I plug in numbers? When there's an expression with a letter and the choices are numbers. When there are letters in the choices. When the amount doesn't matter, like in a ratio. And when there are more letters than equations.
at: when do I plug in numbers

slides.say: And how? Say which number and why, before you use it. Check that the choices come out different, so when the choices have letters, skip zero and one, because they often make choices tie.
Give different letters different numbers. Rule out three choices, and if two are left, use a tie-breaker number. And remember, it's your safety net.
It's the most important technique on the exam, so practice it a lot. Now let's see it in sample questions. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next video.
